stages.title: Ship resistance
stages.hook: A ferry doubles its speed. Does it need twice the engine power? Make a prediction first.
explain: As a ship moves, the water and air push back. This total resistance R has several parts. Frictional resistance comes from water rubbing along the hull. Wave-making resistance is the energy used to create the ship's own waves. Form (pressure) resistance comes from the hull shape, and air resistance acts on the part above water.

The power needed just to tow the hull is the effective power P_E = R × V, with R in newtons and V in m/s giving watts. Resistance grows roughly with speed squared, so power grows roughly with speed cubed. Wave-making rises even faster at high speed, so the last few knots are very costly in fuel.

The Froude number Fr = V ÷ √(g L) compares speed with hull length. When Fr rises above about 0.3 wave-making grows strongly. Long slim hulls make smaller waves at a given speed, a smooth coating reduces friction, and a bulbous bow can cancel some waves. Less resistance means less fuel and less pollution.

example.q: A ship has total resistance 200 kN at 10 m/s. What is its effective power?

analogies.sport: A cyclist feels the air push harder the faster they go, and needs much more effort for a small speed gain.
analogies.home: Moving your hand slowly through bath water is easy; moving it fast is tiring, because resistance rises fast.
analogies.sea: A canoe leaves a small wave, a big fast launch leaves a large wake. The wake is energy wasted.
analogies.tech: A smooth hull coating works like a polished slide: less rubbing, less energy lost.

stages.mnemonic: FWFA: Friction, Wave, Form, Air. Power = Resistance × Velocity.

stages.limits: The square and cube rules are approximations. Real ships have friction that scales a little less than V², and wave resistance that changes sharply with speed.

stages.title: Ship propulsion
stages.hook: A propeller spins inside the water. How does spinning blades push a giant ship forward?
explain: A propeller works like a rotating wing. Each blade is shaped to push water backward. By Newton's third law the water pushes the blade, and the ship, forward. This push is the thrust.

Power flows from the engine to the water through steps, each losing some. Brake power at the engine passes through the gearbox and shaft to the propeller. The delivered power P_D at the propeller is related to the effective power by P_D = P_E ÷ η_D, where η_D is the quasi-propulsive coefficient, often about 0.6 to 0.7.

Propeller pitch is the distance it would advance in one turn in a solid. The ideal advance per second is pitch × revolutions per second, but water gives way, so a real propeller slips. If the blade pressure gets too low the water boils into bubbles: this is cavitation, which causes noise, vibration and damage to blades, and noise that harms marine life. Other devices include azimuth thrusters that rotate, water jets, and sails or rotor sails that save fuel.

example.q: A propeller has pitch 4 m and turns at 120 rpm. What is the ideal advance speed, with no slip?

analogies.home: A screw moves forward into wood by a set amount each turn. A propeller is like a screw in water, but water slips.
analogies.farm: A tractor with wheelspin in mud moves less than its wheels turn, like propeller slip.
analogies.sport: A rower's oar pushes water back to move the boat forward.
analogies.tech: A drone's rotor pushes air down to lift. A propeller pushes water backward.

stages.title: Vessel stability and motions
stages.hook: Why does a ship roll gently on a long swell but sometimes lurch badly in waves that seem smaller?
explain: A floating vessel can move in six ways: three translations (surge forward-back, sway sideways, heave up-down) and three rotations (roll about the long axis, pitch about the side-to-side axis, yaw about the vertical axis). Together these are the six degrees of freedom.

For roll, a ship behaves like a pendulum with a natural period T_φ = 2π k ÷ √(g × GM), where k is the radius of gyration (about 0.35 to 0.4 of the beam B) and GM is the metacentric height. Large GM gives short periods and snappy rolls; small GM gives slow, lazy rolls. If waves reach the ship at about the same period, resonance builds large rolls.

Stability also changes when weight moves. If a mass w is moved sideways a distance d on a ship of displacement Δ, the centre of gravity shifts by GG₁ = w × d ÷ Δ, and the ship heels to angle θ where tan θ = GG₁ ÷ GM. Shifting cargo, loose water on deck, strong wind and sharp turns can all produce dangerous heel, so ships carry stability booklets and loading computers.

example.q: 50 t is moved 10 m sideways on a 5000 t ship with GM = 1.0 m. Find the heel angle.

analogies.home: A child on a swing goes high if pushed at just the right rhythm. That is resonance, like waves matching a ship's roll period.
analogies.sport: A skateboarder on a half-pipe rocks back and forth at a natural rhythm.
analogies.city: A tall building sways in wind with a natural period, which designers try to avoid matching with wind gusts.
analogies.farm: A trailer with a loose load of grain sloshing from side to side can start to lean badly.

The time of one free oscillation of the ship.

misc.wrong: More stability always means a safer, more comfortable ship.
misc.right: Very high GM gives a short roll period, which is violent for people and cargo. Designers aim for enough but not too much stability.

stages.limits: These are small-angle formulas for still water. Real ships in waves need computer calculations, and large heel needs the full GZ curve.

stages.title: Offshore wave loading
stages.hook: A single vertical pipe stands in the sea. How would you calculate how hard waves push on it?
explain: A wave pushes on a structure in two main ways. The drag force is like wind on a flag: water moving past the pipe pushes it. The inertia force comes from accelerating water, like pushing a heavy mass that is speeding up and slowing down. The Morison equation adds them for a slender vertical cylinder, per metre of length: F = ½ ρ C_D D u|u| + ρ C_M (π D² ÷ 4) a.

Here ρ = 1025 kg/m³, D is the pipe diameter, u is water velocity, a is water acceleration, C_D is the drag coefficient (about 1 for a rough cylinder) and C_M is the inertia coefficient (about 2). The Morison equation works when the member is slender, roughly D < λ ÷ 5. For a huge column, the structure changes the waves (diffraction) and other methods are needed.

Water velocity in a wave is largest at the surface and falls with depth. Drag is biggest when velocity peaks (under a crest) and inertia is biggest when acceleration peaks (between crest and trough), so the two forces are out of step in time. The total force on a platform is the sum over all members, and engineers use the design wave from storm statistics. Waves can also slam on decks, so decks are set above the crest.

example.q: A pile has D = 1 m. Water moves at 2 m/s. With C_D = 1.0 and ρ = 1025 kg/m³, find the drag force per metre length.
steps: F = ½ ρ C_D D u².

analogies.home: Holding your hand out of a moving car, the push on it is like drag, and it grows quickly with speed.
analogies.sport: Catching a fast ball is a mix of the ball's speed and how quickly it slows in your hands.
analogies.city: A bridge pier in a flowing river feels the water push all along its length.
analogies.tech: Wind engineers use almost the same formulas for wind on a chimney.

stages.limits: The coefficients vary with roughness (like marine growth), Reynolds number and wave conditions. Engineers choose them from tests and standards, not a single exact value.

stages.title: Offshore structural concepts
stages.hook: A platform in 50 m of water and one in 1500 m of water cannot be built the same way. Why not?
explain: Offshore structures come in two families: fixed and floating. Fixed structures stand on the sea bed. A jacket is a steel lattice frame held by piles. A gravity-based structure (GBS) is a huge concrete base that stays in place by its own weight. Both are strong but become very expensive in deep water.

A compliant tower is a slim tower that bends with the waves. In deep water floating concepts take over. A semi-submersible has columns and pontoons below the surface. A spar is a deep vertical cylinder. A tension-leg platform (TLP) is a floating platform pulled down by vertical tendons so it hardly heaves. An FPSO (floating production, storage and offloading vessel) is a ship that processes and stores oil.

The choice depends on depth, waves, soil, field size, what is produced and cost. A TLP floats with excess buoyancy: buoyant force minus weight is the tendon pretension. If the tendons go slack, the platform loses control, so designers check this carefully. Wind turbines use their own concepts: monopiles in shallow water and floating foundations for deep sites.

example.q: A TLP displaces 70 000 m³ of sea water and its weight (mass) is 60 000 t. Find the total tendon pretension. (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)

analogies.sea: An FPSO is a ship that is also a floating factory and storage tank.
analogies.farm: A gravity base is like a heavy fence post set in a concrete block.
analogies.city: A tall building uses deep foundations, like piles for a jacket.

stages.title: Subsea pipeline fundamentals
stages.hook: A pipe on the sea bed carries gas at 15 times the pressure of a car tyre. How thick must the steel be so it does not burst?
explain: A pressurised pipe tries to split along its length. The stress in the wall around the circumference is the hoop stress σ = p × D ÷ (2 × t), where p is internal pressure, D the diameter and t the wall thickness. Thicker walls or smaller diameter lower the stress. Designers keep σ below a fraction of the steel's yield strength, and add extra thickness for corrosion.

Outside the pipe, water pressure acts too. Deep, empty or low-pressure pipes may collapse or buckle, so external pressure checks matter. On the sea bed, pipes must also stay in place against currents, so concrete coating adds weight. Free spans, where the pipe bridges a dip, can vibrate in current and suffer fatigue.

Corrosion is controlled with coatings and cathodic protection from sacrificial anodes. Pigs, devices pushed through the pipe by the flow, clean it and inspect it. Pipes are laid by S-lay (a long ramp), J-lay (near-vertical, for deep water) or reel-lay (spooled steel pipe). Routes avoid reefs and fishing areas, and leak detection and shut-down valves protect the sea.

example.q: p = 15 MPa, D = 0.5 m and t = 0.02 m. Find the hoop stress.

analogies.home: A balloon bursts first where the rubber is thinnest, as a pipe would at a thin spot.
analogies.farm: A bucket with a band around it: the band feels tension from the water pushing outward, like hoop stress.
analogies.sport: Cyclists pump tyres to high pressure, and strong tyres have thicker walls.
analogies.tech: A pig is like a robot that travels along the pipe cleaning and checking.

stages.mnemonic: Hoop stress = p D over 2 t: more pressure, bigger pipe, thinner wall means more stress.
terms: Stress around the circumference of a pressurised pipe.
A section of pipe that is not supported by the sea bed.
Protecting steel by making it the cathode, e.g. with anodes.
A device sent through a pipeline to clean or inspect it.

misc.wrong: A thicker pipe is always better.
misc.right: Thicker pipe costs more, is heavier to lay, and may be harder to weld. Engineers choose the thickness the loads require, plus allowances.

stages.limits: The hoop stress formula is for thin-walled pipes. Real codes include safety factors, temperature, external pressure and installation loads.

teach.topic: Why pipeline walls have to be thick enough
teach.model: Pressure inside a pipe pulls the wall apart around its circumference. The stress is pressure times diameter divided by twice the thickness. So engineers pick a thickness that keeps stress safely below the steel's strength, and add protection against corrosion.

stages.title: Marine geotechnics
stages.hook: A heavy structure sits on the sea bed. What decides whether it sinks into the mud or stays put?
explain: Marine geotechnics studies sea-bed soils. Soils are mainly clay (tiny, sticky particles), sand (larger grains) and silt in between. Clay strength is described by undrained shear strength s_u; sand strength depends on friction angle.

Soil is made of grains with water in the gaps. Effective stress σ' is the stress carried by the grains: σ' = σ − u, where u is the pore water pressure. Under water, the grains are lifted by buoyancy, so effective unit weight is γ' = γ_sat − γ_w, where γ_w ≈ 10 kN/m³. Soil strength depends on effective stress, which is why saturated sand can suddenly lose strength if the pore pressure rises during shaking (liquefaction).

A foundation resting on clay has a bearing capacity roughly q_u = N_c × s_u, with N_c about 6 for a circular or square footing (a stated assumption). The structure's load divided by its area must stay well below q_u, with a safety factor of at least 2 or 3. Surveys use boreholes, cone penetration tests and samples taken from ships.

example.q: Saturated soil has γ_sat = 18 kN/m³. Take γ_w = 10 kN/m³. Find the effective vertical stress at 5 m depth.

analogies.home: Wet sand at the beach is firm when still, but if you shake it hard it turns soupy, like liquefaction.
analogies.farm: A tractor sinks into soft wet clay and not onto dry gravel.
analogies.sport: Stud spacing on football boots spreads the load; a wide footing spreads a structure's weight.
analogies.sea: A mud-mat is like snow-shoes: wide so you do not sink.

stages.mnemonic: Soil carries load through grains: effective stress is total minus water.
terms: Strength of clay used for short-term loading, s_u.
Stress carried by the soil grains, total stress minus pore pressure.
The largest pressure a soil can carry before failure.
Loss of strength in saturated soil when pore pressure rises.

misc.wrong: Sea-bed soil is the same everywhere in an area.
misc.right: Soil can change quickly over short distances, so each site needs its own survey.

stages.limits: Soil behaviour is complex and uncertain. Values like N_c depend on shape, depth and soil layers; designers use codes and safety factors.

stages.title: Mooring systems
stages.hook: A floating platform weighing thousands of tonnes sits above 1000 m of water. What holds it from drifting away?
explain: A mooring system holds a floating structure near its position against wind, waves and current. It has a fairlead on the vessel, lines of chain, steel wire or synthetic rope, and anchors on the sea bed.

In a catenary mooring the line hangs in a curve and part lies on the sea bed. Its weight gives a restoring force: when the vessel is pushed away, more line lifts off the bed and the pull grows. For a line with submerged weight w per metre in water depth d, the tension at the fairlead is T = H + w × d, where H is the horizontal tension. Taut mooring lines are stretched at an angle and use stretchy polyester rope, which works better in deep water.

Anchor types include drag-embedment anchors, suction piles (a large upturned bucket sucked into the clay), and driven piles. The strength of the line is the minimum breaking load (MBL). Design requires a safety factor, usually well above 1.5 for intact conditions and checks for one broken line. Mooring lines wear by fatigue and corrosion, so they are inspected.

example.q: A catenary line has w = 1500 N/m in d = 100 m of water. If H = 300 kN, find the fairlead tension.

analogies.home: A hanging washing line sags: pull the ends apart and the sag lessens as the tension rises.
analogies.farm: A tethered goat can wander a bit but the rope pulls it back, as moorings do.
analogies.sport: A bungee cord stretches and then pulls back, like a taut polyester mooring.
analogies.sea: A small boat at anchor swings with wind and tide.

stages.mnemonic: T equals H plus w times d: tension at the top is pull sideways plus hanging weight.

The curve of a hanging line.
An anchor like an upturned bucket pushed into the sea bed by suction.
Minimum breaking load of a line.

misc.wrong: A mooring holds the platform perfectly still.
misc.right: Moorings allow some motion (offset) and rely on restoring forces. Too stiff a system would break; too soft would allow drifting.

stages.limits: The simple catenary formula ignores line stretch, current on the line and dynamic effects. Real analysis uses software that checks time histories.

stages.title: Offshore installation fundamentals
stages.hook: How do you lift a 500-tonne module onto a platform from a ship that is itself rocking on the waves?
explain: Offshore installation moves large structures from a yard to the sea and fixes them in place. Common stages are load-out (moving onto a barge), sea fastening (securing for the voyage), transport, lifting or launching, and connection. Each stage has its own risks, weather limits and procedures.

Lifts are planned with a safety margin. Because the vessel and crane move, the load can jerk. The hook load is multiplied by a dynamic amplification factor (DAF), for example 1.3, to give the design load. Slings spread weight, and the tension in each depends on the angle: for two slings at angle θ to the horizontal, T = W ÷ (2 sin θ). Steeper slings (larger θ) carry less tension than shallow ones, so shallow slings need stronger rigging.

The splash zone, where a lifted object enters or leaves the water, is dangerous because waves slam on the load. Heavy-lift vessels, jack-up vessels (which stand on legs) and float-overs (placing a deck by lowering a barge with ballast) are used. Piles may be driven with hammers, and noise controls like bubble curtains protect marine animals. A weather window is chosen using forecasts, and work stops if limits are exceeded.

example.q: A 500 t module is lifted with DAF = 1.3. Find the design hook load. (g = 9.81 m/s²)

analogies.home: Carrying a heavy bag while walking, each step jerks the load. The extra effort is like the DAF.
analogies.farm: A tractor lifting a bale on a bumpy field feels extra load from the bumps.
analogies.city: A crane on a building site: workers wait if the wind is too strong.
analogies.sport: A weightlifter needs the barbell steady; a rocking boat makes this much harder.

The region where waves hit a load entering or leaving the water.
A period with calm enough weather for the operation.
Securing cargo on a vessel for sea transport.

misc.wrong: If a lift is within the crane's rating on the dock, it is safe at sea.
misc.right: At sea the crane base moves with waves, so loads can be much higher than static weight. Sea state limits and a DAF are essential.

stages.limits: DAF values depend on sea state, vessel and lifting method. Operations are simulated and may be stopped if forecast limits are passed.

questions.q: Why is lowering a load through the splash zone especially risky?
questions.model: In the splash zone waves slam on the load and the vessel and crane are moving, so the sling forces can suddenly jump or go slack and snap tight. This causes big dynamic loads, so limits and slow, controlled lowering are used.
questions.why: Wave impact plus vessel motion produces large changing forces.

panel.q: A heavy-lift vessel's crane has a lower rated capacity at a longer outreach. Why?

The crane is lighter when it reaches out

teach.topic: How a heavy module is lifted at sea
